historical_record.description: The Japanese Tea Garden dates from 1894; it has been determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places.

Answering the Council for Civic Unity and a Board of Supervisors resolution, the Recreation and Park Commission recorded that it had no objection in principle to restoring the name "Japanese" Tea Garden to what was then the Oriental Tea Garden, provided the change cost its lessee nothing and had his consent.

Urged by the Consulate General of Japan and the Japanese American community, and noting the peace treaty with Japan, the Recreation and Park Commission unanimously voted to restore the name Japanese Tea Garden, to take effect on April 7, 1953, when the lease was renewed.

Asked by the California Historical Society and women's clubs, the Recreation and Park Commission directed that a memorial plaque to George Turner Marsh, who built the original tea garden for the Midwinter Fair, be designed for the Japanese Tea Garden and funded in the next year's budget.

The Japanese Tea Garden's gates, restored by a team of master craftsmen from Japan, were rededicated on September 3, 1985; department crews also repaired the irrigation, repainted the bridges and cleaned and painted the pagoda.
The Recreation and Park Commission approved the wording of five bronze information plaques for the Japanese Tea Garden, on its dwarf tree collection, pagoda and Zen garden among other features.

The Hagiwara family, who had cared for the garden for nearly half a century and developed the training of its dwarf trees, were forced to leave with all Japanese on the West Coast, and their tree collection was entrusted to Samuel Newsom, as the garden's plaque records.
The garden's pagoda came from the Japanese exhibit of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, as the garden's plaque records.
The garden's Zen garden was designed by Nagao Sakurai, a leading landscape architect of Japan, as the garden's plaque records.

The Hagiwara-Fraser collection of dwarf trees, bequeathed back to the garden by Dr. Hugh Fraser's widow, was planted on Waterfall Hill to a design by the landscape architect Samuel Newsom, as the garden's plaque records.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved replacing the Japanese Tea Garden's exit gate, in place at the garden's west end since 1940, and screening its turnstile with a Japanese-style enclosure with a raised roof and a higher gate, paid for from the balance of the gate restoration fund.

M. Hagiwara, who held the Japanese Tea Garden in Golden Gate Park, asked the Board of Park Commissioners for permission to put up a real Japanese temple in the proposed new tea garden, its site subject to the board's approval; the board left it to Superintendent McLaren with full power to act.

The Imperial Japanese Commission sent the Board of Park Commissioners the keys of the temple and the special exhibit hall in the Japanese gardens at the Panama-Pacific Exposition, donated to Golden Gate Park; the board had no money to move the buildings and referred the matter to Superintendent McLaren.

The extension of the Japanese Garden was nearly finished: a chain of ponds at different levels joined by rocky channels, puddled with clay from Buena Vista Park and lined with concrete, edged with lichen-covered rock from Pinole and Ingleside; a fence, two gateways, a temple to Buddha on the small hill and a tea house above the large lake were to complete it.
